subsystems.name: Metamaterial unit cell
subsystems.role: the sub-wavelength building block that bends waves the wrong way.

subsystems.name: Cloaking shell
subsystems.role: arranges unit cells in a graded pattern that guides waves around the hidden object.

subsystems.name: Design and simulation
subsystems.role: computes the required material properties from transformation optics.

subsystems.name: Fabrication toolchain
subsystems.role: makes the tiny structures accurately and at the right scale.

subsystems.name: Characterisation setup
subsystems.role: measures whether the cloak actually works.

buildSteps.title: Choose the target waveband and object size
buildSteps.detail: Decide which frequencies to cloak (e.g. radar microwaves, infrared, visible light) and the dimensions of the object, since the cloak must be many wavelengths across to hide it.

buildSteps.title: Run transformation optics
buildSteps.detail: Solve for the spatial map of permittivity and permeability that would bend incoming rays smoothly around the object and restore them on the far side.

buildSteps.title: Design unit cells
buildSteps.detail: Engineer sub-wavelength resonators whose response reproduces the required local values at the chosen frequency.

buildSteps.title: Simulate the full cloak
buildSteps.detail: Use electromagnetic solvers to check that the assembled shell hides the object across the intended band, adjusting the design for losses and reflections.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the elements
buildSteps.detail: Pattern metal and dielectric layers with lithography or self-assembly to form the resonators; stack them into a three-dimensional shell.

buildSteps.title: Assemble the shell
buildSteps.detail: Position the elements around the object, often layer by layer, maintaining the designed gradient.

buildSteps.title: Test in a controlled environment
buildSteps.detail: Measure scattering and shadow with the cloak on and off, in an anechoic chamber for microwaves or an optical testbed for light.

buildSteps.title: Integrate and field-test
buildSteps.detail: Attach the cloak to the real object and check performance under realistic angles, polarisations and backgrounds.

prerequisites.why: demonstrated at microwave frequencies, but low-loss operation at infrared and visible wavelengths remains hard.
mathematical framework is well established and used to specify cloaking shells.
electron-beam lithography and related tools can make the needed features, but scaling to large 3D shells is slow and expensive.
metal resonators absorb energy, so most cloaks are lossy and narrowband.
current designs work only over a narrow frequency range, while real stealth or privacy needs wide bands.
cloaks have been shown only for objects a few wavelengths across, not for aircraft or buildings.

pathway.milestone: microwave cloaks demonstrated in laboratories for small objects
pathway.unlocks: proof that the physics works, and testbeds for design tools.

pathway.milestone: infrared and visible cloaks at microscopic scales
pathway.unlocks: applications in microscopy and sensing where hiding a probe is useful.

pathway.milestone: adaptive or active cloaks that sense and cancel scattered waves
pathway.unlocks: wider bandwidth and tolerance to changing angles.

pathway.milestone: practical stealth or privacy cloaks at useful sizes
pathway.unlocks: military stealth, private communications, or architectural privacy — if losses, bandwidth and fabrication are solved.
